This argument is not made lightly. Targeting critical infrastructure raises serious ethical, legal, and strategic questions that deserve honest engagement. However, a careful analysis of the current threat landscape, the logic of deterrence, the comparative advantages of cyber operations over kinetic alternatives, and the dangerous consequences of restraint reveals that offensive cyber readiness is not merely advisable—it is an urgent national imperative.

I. The Threat Landscape Demands an Offensive Posture

To understand why the United States must adopt an aggressive offensive cyber posture, one must first appreciate the gravity of the threats it faces. The era of American cyber vulnerability is not hypothetical; it is already here.

Russia has repeatedly demonstrated both the capability and willingness to use cyber weapons against critical infrastructure. The 2015 and 2016 attacks on Ukraine's power grid—attributed to Russian military intelligence (GRU)—left hundreds of thousands of civilians without electricity and served as proof-of-concept operations for what Russia could do to a NATO member or the United States itself. The SolarWinds intrusion of 2020 compromised multiple U.S. federal agencies and major corporations, constituting one of the most significant intelligence breaches in American history. The NotPetya attack of 2017, while nominally targeted at Ukraine, caused over $10 billion in global damages, crippling Maersk's shipping operations, Merck's pharmaceutical production, and FedEx's logistics systems. This was, in effect, an act of economic warfare conducted with plausible deniability.

China has engaged in decades of sustained cyber espionage and pre-positioning operations against American infrastructure. The Volt Typhoon campaign, publicly exposed in 2023, revealed that Chinese state-sponsored hackers had embedded themselves within U.S. critical infrastructure networks—including water treatment facilities, power systems, and transportation networks—not for intelligence collection, but for potential disruption or destruction during a future conflict, particularly one involving Taiwan. FBI Director Christopher Wray testified before Congress that Chinese hackers had pre-positioned capabilities to "wreak havoc and cause real-world harm to American citizens and communities." This is not espionage; it is the preparation of a battlefield.

Iran launched destructive attacks against Saudi Aramco in 2012, wiping data from 30,000 computers. It has targeted American banks, a dam in New York State, and municipal systems. North Korea conducted the WannaCry ransomware attack that paralyzed the UK's National Health Service and extorted institutions worldwide.

The common thread is unmistakable: America's adversaries are already waging cyber campaigns against critical infrastructure, pre-positioning destructive capabilities, and treating cyberspace as an active theater of conflict. For the United States to refrain from developing and demonstrating comparable—and superior—offensive capabilities is not restraint; it is unilateral disarmament in a domain where adversaries are already armed and aggressive.

II. The Logic of Deterrence Applies to Cyberspace

The foundational logic of deterrence is straightforward: an adversary will refrain from aggressive action if it believes the costs of that action will exceed the benefits. This principle has underpinned global stability for decades—most notably through nuclear deterrence, which, whatever its moral complexities, has prevented great-power war for nearly eighty years.

Deterrence requires three elements: capability, credibility, and communication. The United States must possess offensive cyber capabilities sufficient to impose unacceptable costs on adversaries; it must be credibly willing to use those capabilities; and adversaries must know both of these things.

Currently, American cyber deterrence suffers from critical weaknesses in all three areas. While U.S. Cyber Command possesses significant capabilities, the persistent reluctance to use them—or even to publicly acknowledge specific offensive operations—undermines credibility. Adversaries have repeatedly attacked American interests in cyberspace with minimal consequences. Russia faced no meaningful cyber retaliation for SolarWinds. China has faced no operational consequences for Volt Typhoon's infrastructure pre-positioning. Iran and North Korea have continued their campaigns with impunity.

This pattern of restraint does not project wisdom or moral superiority; it projects weakness, and weakness invites aggression. As political scientist Robert Jervis demonstrated in his seminal work on deterrence theory, a failure to respond to provocations signals to adversaries that future provocations will also be tolerated, encouraging escalatory behavior.

The development and declared willingness to deploy offensive cyber capabilities against adversary infrastructure would fundamentally alter this calculus. If Chinese military planners know that an attack on Taiwan could trigger the disruption of China's financial clearing systems, the destabilization of its power grid, or the compromise of its industrial control networks, the expected costs of aggression increase dramatically. If Russian strategists understand that a cyber attack on American infrastructure would be met with a proportional or escalatory response against Russian systems, the calculus shifts toward restraint.

Some argue that cyber deterrence is inherently unstable because attribution is difficult and capabilities are uncertain. This objection, while worthy of consideration, is increasingly outdated. Attribution capabilities have improved significantly; the United States and its allies have publicly attributed major operations with high confidence. Moreover, deterrence does not require perfect attribution in every case—it requires that adversaries believe they will likely be identified and punished. The shift toward what General Paul Nakasone, former commander of U.S. Cyber Command, called "persistent engagement" and "defending forward" reflects a growing recognition within the defense establishment that passive defense is insufficient and that the U.S. must operate continuously in adversary networks.

III. Offensive Cyber Operations Are More Humane Than the Alternatives

One of the most powerful arguments for offensive cyber capabilities targeting infrastructure is the comparative humanitarian case. In any serious confrontation between great powers, the alternatives to cyber operations are kinetic military actions: bombing campaigns, missile strikes, naval blockades, and ground invasions. These alternatives kill people—often in large numbers, including civilians.

A cyber operation that disables an adversary's power grid or disrupts its financial systems causes economic pain, confusion, and hardship, but it does not, in the immediate sense, kill anyone. The effects are often reversible. Systems can be restored. The physical infrastructure remains intact. Compare this to the firebombing of Dresden, the nuclear destruction of Hiroshima, or even the precision-guided munitions campaigns of the Gulf Wars, which, despite their accuracy, killed thousands of civilians.

If the United States faces a situation in which it must compel an adversary to change course—whether to deter an invasion of a treaty ally, to respond to an attack on American interests, or to prevent a humanitarian catastrophe—having the option to impose costs through cyber means rather than kinetic means is not merely strategically advantageous. It is the morally preferable choice. To deny policymakers this option by refusing to develop these capabilities is to guarantee that future crises will be resolved through bloodier means.

Furthermore, the preemptive development and positioning of these capabilities may prevent conflict altogether. If deterrence succeeds—if China does not invade Taiwan, if Russia does not attack a NATO member, if Iran does not close the Strait of Hormuz—then the offensive cyber capabilities will have achieved their purpose without ever being used. This is precisely how nuclear deterrence has functioned: the weapons exist to ensure they are never needed.

IV. Preemptive Positioning Is a Strategic Necessity

Critics may accept the need for offensive cyber capabilities in principle but object to the preemptive nature of the proposed posture. This objection reflects a misunderstanding of how cyber operations work.

Unlike conventional military operations, cyber weapons cannot be developed and deployed on demand. Offensive cyber operations require months or years of intelligence preparation: mapping adversary networks, identifying vulnerabilities, developing exploits, establishing persistent access, and testing tools. If the United States waits until a crisis erupts to begin this process, it will be too late. The window of strategic need will have closed before the capability is ready.

This reality is well understood by America's adversaries. China's Volt Typhoon campaign is explicitly a pre-positioning operation designed to ensure that destructive cyber capabilities are ready for use the moment a conflict begins. Russia has pre-positioned access in European energy networks. If the United States does not engage in comparable pre-positioning, it enters any future crisis at a severe disadvantage—with adversaries holding a loaded weapon while American cyber forces scramble to find the safety on theirs.

Preemptive development and positioning does not mean reckless or unprovoked deployment. It means ensuring that when the President of the United States faces a crisis, the full spectrum of options is available—including options that are less destructive and less lethal than the kinetic alternatives. Military readiness has always required preparation before conflict. The Navy does not wait for war to build aircraft carriers. The Air Force does not wait for an attack to train pilots. Cyber Command should not wait for a crisis to establish the access and tools necessary for effective operations.

V. Addressing the Objections

Serious objections to this position deserve serious responses.

"Targeting civilian infrastructure is immoral and violates international humanitarian law."

International humanitarian law (IHL) prohibits attacks on civilian objects unless they make an effective contribution to military action and their destruction offers a definite military advantage. In practice, every major power targets dual-use infrastructure during conflict—power grids supply military installations, financial systems fund war efforts, and telecommunications enable military command and control. The United States has targeted electrical systems in every major conflict since World War II. The question is not whether infrastructure will be targeted in a conflict—it will—but whether cyber means are preferable to bombs. They manifestly are.

Moreover, IHL applies to armed conflict, and one of the goals of offensive cyber deterrence is to prevent armed conflict from occurring in the first place. A capability that prevents war is not immoral; it is profoundly moral.

"This will trigger a cyber arms race."

The cyber arms race is already underway. China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, and numerous other states are investing heavily in offensive cyber capabilities. American restraint has not slowed this process; it has merely ensured that the United States falls behind relative to the pace of adversary development and deployment. Unilateral restraint in an arms race is not statesmanship—it is strategic negligence.

"Offensive cyber operations risk escalation to conventional or nuclear conflict."

This is the most serious objection, and it demands careful consideration. Escalation is a genuine risk in any domain of military competition. However, this risk argues for careful doctrine, clear communication, and graduated response options—not for the abandonment of offensive capability. Indeed, having a spectrum of cyber options available makes escalation less likely, because policymakers can respond to provocations proportionally without resorting to kinetic force. A president with no cyber options faces a stark choice between acquiescence and military strikes; a president with offensive cyber capabilities can calibrate a response precisely.

Furthermore, the historical record suggests that cyber operations have not escalated to kinetic conflict. Russia's attacks on Ukraine's grid did not trigger a conventional military response. The Stuxnet operation against Iran's nuclear program did not lead to war. The cyber domain, far from being uniquely escalatory, appears to offer a space for strategic competition below the threshold of armed conflict—precisely the kind of competition the United States should be prepared to win.

"Norms of restraint benefit the United States because it is more dependent on digital infrastructure."

This argument holds that because the United States is more digitally interconnected than its adversaries, it has more to lose from the normalization of infrastructure attacks. There is some truth to this, but it leads to the wrong conclusion. The greater vulnerability of American infrastructure is an argument for better defense and more credible deterrence—not for unilateral restraint. If the United States is uniquely vulnerable, then the consequences of failed deterrence are uniquely severe, which makes effective deterrence uniquely important.

Norms of restraint are only valuable if adversaries respect them. As the evidence demonstrates, they do not. China is already inside American infrastructure. Russia has already attacked allied infrastructure. Clinging to norms that adversaries violate with impunity does not protect the United States; it constrains it while leaving adversaries free to act.

VI. A Framework for Responsible Offensive Cyber Operations

Advocating for offensive cyber capabilities does not mean advocating for their reckless or indiscriminate use. The United States should develop a clear doctrinal framework that governs the development and employment of these capabilities:

  1. Proportionality: Cyber operations against infrastructure should be proportional to the threat faced and calibrated to achieve specific strategic objectives.

  2. Discrimination: Operations should target systems with military significance or dual-use functionality, minimizing effects on purely civilian services such as hospitals and emergency response systems where possible.

  3. Reversibility: Where feasible, operations should be designed to produce temporary and reversible effects rather than permanent destruction.

  4. Authorization: Preemptive deployment in peacetime should require presidential authorization with appropriate congressional notification, consistent with existing frameworks for covert action.

  5. Escalation management: Doctrine should include clear off-ramps and communication channels to prevent unintended escalation.

  6. Alliance integration: Offensive capabilities should be coordinated with allies to strengthen collective deterrence and ensure interoperability.

This framework ensures that offensive cyber capabilities are wielded responsibly, consistent with American values and strategic interests, while maintaining the flexibility necessary for effective deterrence.

VII. The Cost of Inaction

Finally, it is essential to confront the cost of the alternative. If the United States fails to develop and credibly demonstrate its willingness to deploy offensive cyber capabilities against adversary infrastructure, the consequences are foreseeable and grave:

  • Adversaries will continue to pre-position destructive capabilities in American infrastructure with impunity, confident that no comparable threat hangs over their own systems.
  • Deterrence will continue to erode, increasing the likelihood of both cyber and conventional conflict.
  • In a future crisis—over Taiwan, over the Baltic states, over the South China Sea—the United States will face adversaries who possess cyber capabilities ready for immediate deployment while American forces lack equivalent options.
  • The eventual use of force in such a crisis will be kinetic, not cyber, resulting in greater destruction and loss of life.
  • American credibility as a security guarantor will decline, weakening alliances and encouraging nuclear proliferation as allies seek their own deterrents.

The path of restraint leads not to peace but to vulnerability, and vulnerability leads to conflict on terms not of America's choosing.

Conclusion

The development of offensive cyber capabilities designed to target adversary critical infrastructure is not an act of aggression; it is an act of prudence. It reflects the same strategic logic that has underpinned American security for decades: that peace is best preserved by strength, that deterrence requires credible capability, and that the best way to prevent war is to ensure that adversaries understand the costs of starting one.

The cyber domain is now as consequential as land, sea, air, and space. America's adversaries have already weaponized it. They are inside American networks, preparing for a conflict they believe may come. For the United States to meet this reality with anything less than full offensive preparedness—including the preemptive development and positioning of capabilities against adversary infrastructure—would be a historic failure of strategic vision.

The question is not whether offensive cyber operations against critical infrastructure are desirable in the abstract. The question is whether, in a world where adversaries are already waging this form of warfare, the United States can afford to refrain. The answer, clearly and urgently, is that it cannot.

3. Integrated Deterrence Signaling. Our adversaries must understand our capabilities and our willingness to use them. There are those who will say that what I'm proposing is aggressive, that it is provocative, that it crosses a line. And to them I say: the line has already been crossed — by our adversaries, repeatedly, and with growing boldness.

Every day that an American water treatment facility sits with Chinese malware dormant in its control systems is a day that American lives are held hostage by a foreign power. Every day that we fail to impose costs is a day that the calculus of aggression tilts further against us.

We have a moral obligation to defend the American people — not just to respond after they've been harmed, but to prevent that harm from occurring when we have the intelligence and the capability to do so.

The United States did not become the guarantor of global stability by hoping for the best. We became it by ensuring that those who would threaten freedom understood, in the marrow of their bones, that the cost of aggression would be unbearable.

Cyberspace is the battlefield of this century. The infrastructure that sustains modern life — energy, finance, communications, healthcare, transportation — is the strategic terrain. And right now, our adversaries are maneuvering on that terrain with confidence and impunity while we debate whether it's polite to show up.

Enough.

It is time for the United States to bring to the cyber domain the same strategic vision, the same moral courage, and the same overwhelming capability that has defined American power at its best.

Not to start wars — but to prevent them.

Not to harm civilians — but to protect them.

Not to destabilize the world — but to remind it that there are consequences for threatening the nation that has done more than any other in human history to advance the cause of liberty.

The tools are in our hands. The talent exists within our ranks. The threat is at our gates.
